notes:
I've written notes for most verses. I couldn't find anything usable for v. 22, and only a little for vv. 3 and 7. My tools hit their usage limit before I could open the Pulpit, Gill or Ellicott chapter pages in full, or search the Lutheran, Pentecostal, Orthodox and prosperity/word-of-faith sites. Several notes therefore come from search-result excerpts of the biblehub and studylight verse pages, not full pages. Everything below comes only from what I could read.

## Deuteronomy 10: research notes

**v. 1:** Ellicott says this command came before Moses' forty days of pleading for the people (Exod 34:28). God had ordered the ark during the earlier forty days (Exod 25:10). Ellicott rejects Rashi's idea that there were two arks. He thinks Moses may have used a temporary box until Bezalel built the real ark. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/10.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: the ark was ordered before the golden calf. It was only made after the tabernacle was built, and the tablets went in when the tabernacle was dedicated (Exod 40:20). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/deuteronomy/10.htm
- Guzik: Moses broke the first tablets partly in anger, but also as a picture of Israel breaking God's law and covenant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-10/

**v. 2:** Ellicott: it is a common mistake to think Moses wrote the second set himself; the mix-up comes from the shifting "he" in Exod 34:28. He reads the stone tablets as a picture of the heart (2 Cor 3:3). The first tablets stand for Adam's heart before the fall, and the second for the new covenant written on the heart. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/10.htm
- Wesley: the new tablets proved God's anger had turned away. In the same way, God writing his law inside us is the surest proof we are reconciled to him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/deuteronomy-10.html
- Guzik: God made his written word the starting point for the restored relationship. The second tablets show a God who gives failing people a second chance. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-10/

**v. 3:** Keil & Delitzsch give the verse but add nothing beyond the notes at v. 1. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/deuteronomy/10.htm

**v. 4:** Ellicott: the words on the second tablets were exactly the same as on the first. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/10.htm

**v. 5:** Ellicott: Hebrew has no pluperfect, so "the ark which I *had* made" shouldn't mislead readers. "I made" can mean "I had it made," pointing to Bezalel's ark. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/10.htm
- *Catholic:* The Catholic Encyclopedia cites this verse to show the ark was first meant to hold the tablets. In Catholic tradition the ark pictures Christ, and the tablets inside it mean that Christ is the author of the Law. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/01721a.htm and https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/Ark

**vv. 6–7:** Ellicott calls these verses the hardest in Deuteronomy. The route differs from Numbers 20–21 and 33, and Aaron's death happened about 39 years after the events Moses is retelling. His answer is that while going around Edom, Israel passed again through camps they had used before, in a different order. Mosera may have been the district around Mount Hor. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/10.htm
- Ellicott also gives a spiritual reading: Aaron's death points to Christ as a priest "after the power of an endless life." The journey from the "wells" to "a land of rivers of waters" pictures moving from the Law to the Gospel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/10.htm
- Barnes, Geneva and Pulpit: Moserah must have been near Mount Hor, where Numbers says Aaron died. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/10-6.htm
- Why mention Aaron here? Pulpit and Keil & Delitzsch say God kept the high priesthood going in Eleazar despite the golden calf, which was an act of grace. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/10-6.htm
- Wesley says much the same: the passage shows God answered Moses' prayers, and that he made up for Aaron's death by giving Eleazar, who could pray for the people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/deuteronomy-10.html
- Constable: Moserah may not be a place name at all. It could be a common noun meaning "chastisement," giving the reason for Aaron's death. He also counts the water in v. 7 as another sign of God's grace. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/10-10.html
- Guzik: the priesthood is mentioned because Israel needed a go-between to make atonement, pray for them and bless them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-10/
- *Modern scholarship:* The Cambridge Bible marks the wording as "non-deuteronomic." It credits Aaron's death on Mount Hor to the "P" (Priestly) source, one of the separate sources many scholars think make up the Pentateuch. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/10-6.htm
- An answer to the apparent contradiction on preceptaustin says both accounts are true: Mount Hor was probably inside the Moserah area. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-10-commentary

**v. 8:** Wesley: "To stand before the Lord" is the stance of a minister; prophets and angels are described as "standing" too. The Levites blessed the people by God's command and commission. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/deuteronomy-10.html
- Keil & Delitzsch: setting apart Levi was another act of mercy toward Israel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/deuteronomy/10.htm
- Guzik: restoring a relationship with God must always focus on the priestly work of Jesus. He notes the Levites first served as agents of judgment after the golden calf (Exod 32:25–29). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-10/

**v. 9:** Wesley: "The Lord is his inheritance" means the Lord's share, the tithes and offerings, was given to the Levites to live on. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/deuteronomy-10.html
- Preceptaustin: Levi received the best promise of all, the Lord himself. Quoting the ESV Study Bible, it adds that the other tribes had to provide for the landless Levites. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-10-commentary
- GotQuestions: the Levites got cities, not land. God was their inheritance in that they ran the nation's worship. https://www.gotquestions.org/God-inheritance-Levites.html
- *Catholic/Orthodox (early church):* The Apostolic Constitutions applies the Levites' landless status to Christian clergy. It tells bishops they are their people's "priests and Levites," supported by the people's offerings. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/07152.htm
- GotQuestions notes that the word "cleric" comes from the Greek *kleros* ("lot" or "portion"), which links back to this idea. https://www.gotquestions.org/what-is-a-cleric.html
- Guzik, by contrast, points the priesthood to Jesus as mediator (see v. 8).

**v. 10:** Gill links this verse back to v. 5. It describes what happened before Moses came down, and God held back judgment the people deserved. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/10-10.htm
- *Modern scholarship:* The Cambridge Bible surveys theories about where vv. 10–11 fit. One is Steuernagel's view that v. 10 was added by scribes trying to line up the accounts of Moses' prayers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/10-10.htm

**v. 11:** Wesley: it was fitting that the man whose prayers saved the people should lead them. He sees Moses here as a type of Christ, who intercedes for us and has all authority. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/deuteronomy-10.html
- ESV Study Bible (quoted on preceptaustin): the command to set out shows Moses' prayer had been fully answered. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-10-commentary
- Guzik: getting right with God should lead to moving forward, not staying stuck. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-10/

**v. 12:** Calvin: this verse sums up what the whole Law is for. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/10-12.html
- Ellicott quotes Rashi: despite Israel's sin, God asks only for fear of him. He also cites the rabbinic saying that everything is in God's hands "save only the fear of Heaven." https://biblehub.com/deuteronomy/10-12.htm
- Wesley: these duties are owed out of gratitude for great mercies. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/deuteronomy-10.html
- Guzik: this "fear" is reverence, not the kind that runs from God. The love asked for is a decision that answers God's love first (1 John 4:19). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-10/
- GotQuestions compares the verse with Micah 6:8. It says faith that doesn't come from a heart truly devoted to God isn't faith. https://www.gotquestions.org/what-does-God-require-of-us.html
- Keil & Delitzsch: fear of the Lord, which comes from seeing our own sin before a holy God, should be the main thing driving us to obey. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/10-13.htm

**v. 13:** GotQuestions: God's commands are given for our own good, and keeping them shows our love (John 14:15). https://www.gotquestions.org/what-does-God-require-of-us.html
- Preceptaustin: God is not a "cosmic killjoy." His law comes from love and protects his people. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-10-commentary

**v. 14:** Wesley: "heaven of heavens" means the highest, or third, heaven. Since everything belongs to God, he could have chosen any nation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/deuteronomy-10.html
- A sermon outline on preceptaustin: as our Creator, God is owed our thankful lives. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-10-commentary

**v. 15:** Wesley (Methodist): God's choice of the patriarchs came "only from God's good pleasure," not from anything owed to them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/deuteronomy-10.html
- Preceptaustin: the covenant rests on God's love, not on Israel's merit. A NET note it quotes explains that "love" and "choose" are covenant words for God taking the first step. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-10-commentary
- Guzik: being chosen brought Israel both privilege and responsibility. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-10/
- Fruchtenbaum (quoted by Constable): choosing a nation doesn't save every member. Individuals are saved by God's choice and their own faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/10-16.html

**v. 16:** This is the main verse where traditions differ.
- *Common ground:* Commentators of every stripe agree outward circumcision is worthless without a changed heart, often citing Romans 2:28–29. That includes Clarke, Wesley, Gill, Henry, Barnes and Keil & Delitzsch, who says true fear and love of God are impossible without it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/10-16.html and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/10-16.htm
- *Reformed/Calvinist:* Monergism (the view that God alone does the work of salvation) answers the question of how God can command what only he can do. The command shows our inability, as Romans 3:19–20 says the law does, and only grace can fulfil it, as in Deut 30:6, where God promises to circumcise the heart himself. https://www.monergism.com/blog/circumcise-foreskin-your-heart
- Calvin calls it a call to deny oneself and turn from sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/10-16.html
- Gill (Baptist) says it is God's work that only he can do and has promised. He reads the command as making people see their need. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/10-16.htm
- *Methodist:* Wesley simply urges hearers not to rest in outward circumcision but to "seriously set upon" cleansing their hearts. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/deuteronomy-10.html
- *Baptist:* Spurgeon preached vv. 14–16 against the charge that election makes people careless. He argues the command is attached to the doctrine, and being chosen makes people want to be holy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/deuteronomy-10.html
- *Circumcision and baptism:* Some writers apply the verse to baptism: JFB, a sermon outline on biblehub, and the Anglican Archbishop Whately. They say baptism, like circumcision, is worthless as a bare rite without the inner grace. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/10-16.htm and https://biblehub.com/sermons/deuteronomy/10-16.htm
- "Stiff-necked" pictures an ox or donkey resisting its master (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-10/

**v. 17:** Kalland (quoted by Guzik): "God of gods" doesn't mean other gods really exist; it means he is supreme over all. Thompson notes "mighty" is a warrior word. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-10/
- Wesley: God treats Jews and Gentiles alike. Israel shouldn't assume God will overlook its sins because of his kindness to their fathers. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/deuteronomy-10.html
- A devotional on preceptaustin warns not to confuse election with partiality. Partiality twists justice, but God's choice doesn't, "hence the cross." https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-10-commentary

**v. 18:** Wesley: God takes up the cause of the fatherless and widow against powerful enemies, and expects Israel to do the same. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/deuteronomy-10.html

**v. 19:** Merrill (quoted by Guzik): God's people should copy what he does in society, especially toward foreigners, since Israel had been foreigners in Egypt. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-10/
- Matthew Henry: people who have been in trouble and found mercy should be quick to help others in the same trouble. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/10-16.htm

**v. 20:** Wesley: hold fast to God "with firm confidence, true affection, and constant obedience." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/deuteronomy-10.html

**v. 21:** Wesley: "thy praise" means God is the one Israel should praise, and the reason for it (compare Exod 15:2). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/deuteronomy-10.html

**v. 22:** I found nothing.

**Gaps:** I found nothing on 1517.org or lcms.org (Lutheran), on the Pentecostal sites other than Enduring Word, on oca.org (Orthodox), or on Bible Odyssey. I also found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter.
